implementation_notes: For C++ the Golden Hammer is usually a paradigm rather than a library: OOP applied to everything including hot numeric loops, or template metaprogramming applied to a problem that a two-line loop solves, or a hand-rolled framework because the team is expert in writing frameworks. The C++-specific danger of the template form is that the cost is paid at compile time and at compile-time failure, so a build that takes forty minutes is the symptom that no requirement ever justified. The remedy is the same requirement-first comparison, applied to compile time and binary size as first-class requirements alongside runtime performance.
idiom_name: one paradigm applied uniformly (OOP everywhere, or functional everywhere)
pitfalls: Compile time and binary size are requirements nobody writes down, so a metaprogramming hammer is never measured against them.
A hand-rolled framework's value is real but its cost is amortised across the whole team and is invisible to the person who wrote it.
Choosing RAII/smart pointers manually where a simpler ownership model would do, because it is the technique the team is fluent in.
